BEHIND THE EXPERIMENT

When there is
nowhere to hide.

A naked singularity is a theoretical spacetime singularity without an event horizon. Switch between an uncharged Schwarzschild black hole (Q = 0, horizon at r = 2M) and the charged, nonrotating Reissner–Nordström solution with Q/M > 1, in geometric units G = c = 1.

f(r) = 1 − 2M/r + Q²/r²

Each pixel follows a numerically integrated null geodesic. An inward gravitational term and an outward charge term bend its path. For 1 < Q/M ≤ √(9/8), photon spheres can still exist; above that threshold there are no circular photon orbits.

The glowing disk is an artistic, optically thin emitter. It is not a self-consistent accretion model. Cubes are static coordinate-space markers. Finite integration steps and a small central cutoff limit accuracy close to the singularity; this is an exploratory visualization, not a research solver.

Read about Reissner–Nordström naked singularities ↗

Light paths & debug geometry

Choose “Explore light paths” to orbit an external view of rays traced backward from the observer. Bright moving markers illustrate the paths; they are not a coordinate-time animation. Geometry toggles show the center, grid, camera frustum, Schwarzschild reference sphere, and photon spheres. The Schwarzschild radius is a true horizon only in the black-hole mode.

Disk coordinates & comparison

Enable Disk UV debug to match labeled disk regions A1–H4 to the source map. U wraps around the disk; V runs from inner to outer radius. TOP (+Y) uses warm colors; BOTTOM (−Y) uses cool colors. The UV view is an opaque first-intersection diagnostic. Its grid can stay fixed or follow the disk rotation. Compare lensing shows the same observer, time, and scene with curved rays on the left and straight rays on the right. Both views move and pause together.

Falling into a black hole

The descent is a cinematic camera animation with an accelerating radial profile. The final image fades at the event horizon, where the static-observer rendering ends. It is not a physically calibrated free-fall clock or an interior black-hole simulation. Pause, stop, reset, or replay at any time.

Find your way around

Orbit: drag to rotate, scroll or pinch to zoom. Fly: drag to look; W/S forward/back, A/D sideways, Q/E down/up. Hold Shift to move faster. C places a cube ahead of you. F resets the camera. Space pauses animation. Touch: one finger rotates, two fingers zoom.

Your own sky

Upload browser-readable images or Radiance .hdr panoramas. Cube atlases use the order +X, −X, +Y, −Y, +Z, −Z. For six images, use filenames such as px, nx, py, ny, pz, nz (or right, left, top, bottom, front, back). Unrecognized filenames use alphabetical order. Files stay in your browser. The built-in night sky uses NASA/Goddard Deep Star Maps, available at 8K and 16K (subject to your GPU texture limit).
